_readme: State profile for tools/generate_location_pages.py; schema is documented in data/location-state-profiles/IN.json.
name: Ohio

northwest.label: northwest Ohio
climate: {county} County is in the Northwest division of NOAA's ten Ohio climate divisions. A division summary prepared with the Midwest Regional Climate Center describes the climate as continental and driven by the movement of pressure systems across the country. It says summers are generally quite warm in the inland areas and that winters can be cold with moderate to heavy snowfall. The same summary says lake effect reaches the northeastern corner of the division, near Toledo, when winds are easterly.

NOAA's Ohio state climate summary says annual precipitation varies regionally and places the northwestern part of the state, where {county} County sits, on the drier side compared with the southern part. It notes that winter can bring snowstorms and ice storms, and it calls thunderstorms, flood-producing rainstorms, hail and tornadoes common in the warmer months. The summary also reports a significant increase in heavy rain events across Ohio.

NWS Cleveland's report on a January 2016 lake effect event gives snowfall totals ranging from a trace in Toledo to several inches across the snowbelt of northeast Ohio and northwest Pennsylvania. The same report says most of northern Ohio received a light coating of snow from that system. For {county} County, the division summary and this event report together describe a region where lake influence is limited.

north_central.label: north central Ohio
climate: A regional summary for the North Central division, prepared with the Midwest Regional Climate Center, calls its climate primarily continental, with larger temperature ranges than places at the same latitude beside the Great Lakes. It places the division in the snowbelt of northern Ohio, where significant lake-effect snow can occur, and says Lake Erie somewhat tempers temperatures. NOAA's county list assigns {county} County to this division.

NOAA's Ohio state climate summary describes lake-effect snow as the result of arctic air masses warmed and moistened as they cross the Great Lakes. The same summary records that Ohio's deadliest tornado, on June 28, 1924, struck the towns of Sandusky and Lorain, which lie in the North Central division with {county} County. It also states that dangerous storms can occur in every season.

The division summary adds that precipitation is well distributed through the year, with slightly more rain in late spring and early summer. NWS Cleveland's study of El Nino winters found that lake effect snow and orographic effects may mask the El Nino signal in some years at stations near the Great Lakes and the Appalachian Mountains. That study covers the lower Great Lakes, which includes {county} County.

northeast.label: northeast Ohio
climate: The Northeast division, which includes {county} County, has a continental climate with four distinct seasons, according to a summary prepared with the Midwest Regional Climate Center. It describes hot and humid summers and cold, snowy winters. The summary says the division receives abundant lake effect snow from mid-November until ice covers the surface of Lake Erie, which it places in late January or early February.

NWS Cleveland's report on the January 2016 lake effect event says the highest Ohio snowfall totals were recorded in Geauga County, which is in the same NOAA climate division as {county} County. It describes Lake Erie as mostly open water east of the islands, which supplied moisture for a prolonged period of snow under west to northwest winds. It also says lake effect bands vary quickly in intensity over short distances.

In its summary of the 2022-23 winter, NWS Cleveland reports that snowbelt counties east of Cleveland received 30 to 60 inches that winter, against normal amounts of 70 to over 100 inches in those areas. The same summary says the mild winter inhibited ice formation on Lake Erie, and that a mid-March lake effect event added 6 to 10 inches across eastern counties. {county} County is one of the Northeast division counties in NOAA's list.

west_central.label: west central Ohio
climate: NWS Wilmington's summary of April 17, 2024 confirms an EF0 tornado in Champaign County and an EF1 tornado in Delaware County. Champaign County is in the West Central division of NOAA's Ohio climate divisions, alongside {county} County. The same office's summary for that date also mentions large hail and wind, without giving sizes. NOAA's Ohio state climate summary adds that dangerous storms can occur in every season.

NWS Wilmington's summary for March 26, 2026 reports an EF1 tornado near Kenton, in Hardin County, which is part of the West Central division with {county} County. It describes several clusters of thunderstorms that developed ahead of and along a southward-advancing front, in an environment with enough instability and wind shear, and that produced hail, wind and tornadoes. NOAA's Ohio state climate summary puts such storms in context, saying winter can bring snowstorms and ice storms while convective storms are common in the warmer months.

NWS Cleveland's study of El Nino winters says winters in the Ohio Valley and lower Great Lakes averaged warmer than normal during the events it examined. It found a winter precipitation deficit in seven of the eight events studied, and below normal snowfall at many stations, particularly those away from lake effect snow areas. The study region includes {county} County.

central.label: central Ohio
climate: A summary for the Central division, prepared with the Midwest Regional Climate Center, describes a humid continental climate with hot and humid summers and cool to cold winters. It calls precipitation in Ohio moderate compared with the rest of the country, and relatively consistent year-round. It also says severe weather is not uncommon in the division, including tornado threats, and {county} County is one of its counties.

The same Central division summary says gorge-like river valleys near Columbus, particularly along the Scioto and Olentangy, create microclimates that experience distinct weather from the surrounding areas. NOAA's Ohio state climate summary reports that since 2000 Columbus has averaged 22 warm nights per year, against 9 in the 1950s through 1970s. {county} County lies in the same division as Columbus.

NWS Wilmington's summary of April 17, 2024 confirms an EF1 tornado in Delaware County, which is in the Central division with {county} County. NOAA's Ohio state climate summary says dangerous storms can occur in every season, and it lists snowstorms and ice storms among winter weather. It lists thunderstorms, flood-producing rainstorms, hail and tornadoes among the convective storms it calls common in the warmer months.

central_hills.label: the central hills of Ohio
climate: NWS Pittsburgh's severe weather climatology covers Coshocton County, which is in the Central Hills division with {county} County. The climatology looks at tornadoes from 1950 to 2020, severe winds of 58 mph or greater from 1955 to 2019, and hail of 0.75 inch or larger from 1955 to 2019. The office adds that it relies on spotters, broadcast media, cooperative observers, county officials and the public for reports.

NOAA's Ohio state climate summary says annual average temperature in Ohio has risen more than 1.5 degrees F since the beginning of the 20th century and more than 2 degrees F since the 1970s. It adds that the warming has been concentrated in winter and spring, and that summer days have not warmed substantially. {county} County is one of the Central Hills division counties in NOAA's list.

The state summary also reports a significant increase in heavy rain events in Ohio. It records that the Great Flood of 1913 was Ohio's greatest weather disaster and was one of the deadliest floods in U.S. history. It also says winter can bring snowstorms and ice storms, and that dangerous storms can occur in every season, which applies statewide including {county} County.

northeast_hills.label: the northeast hills of Ohio
climate: NWS Pittsburgh's severe weather climatology includes the Ohio counties of Carroll, Columbiana and Harrison, all part of the Northeast Hills division that also contains {county} County. It counts tornadoes from 1950 to 2020, severe winds of 58 mph or greater from 1955 to 2019, and large hail from 1955 to 2019. It also covers Jefferson County in Ohio, and it analyzes each severe weather element by month, by time of day and by year.

The Pittsburgh office notes that the threshold for severe hail changed in 2010 from 0.75 inch to 1.00 inch in diameter, though it still collects reports of hail above 0.75 inch. It states that it remains diligent in documenting every occurrence of severe weather but understands that a lot of cases go unrecorded. Any count for {county} County therefore reflects reports received, not every storm.

NWS Cleveland's El Nino study says lake effect snow and orographic effects may mask the El Nino signal in some years at stations near the Great Lakes and the Appalachian Mountains. The study also found warmer than normal winters across the Ohio Valley and lower Great Lakes during the events it examined. {county} County is within the Northeast Hills division of NOAA's climate list.

southwest.label: southwest Ohio
climate: NOAA's Ohio state climate summary records that the Xenia tornado, rated F5, was part of the Super Outbreak of 1974. Xenia is in Greene County, in the Southwest division that also contains {county} County. The same summary calls the Great Flood of 1913 Ohio's greatest weather disaster, and it states that dangerous storms can occur in every season. It also lists snowstorms and ice storms as winter weather in Ohio.

NWS Wilmington's summary of May 10, 2020 says thunderstorms developed along a cold front in Indiana and moved east across Ohio during the afternoon and early evening. It reports that the storms became strong to severe in many locations, and that additional thunderstorms produced hail across southern Ohio and northern Kentucky. It notes that temperatures were only in the upper 50s to lower 60s, even as the storms became strong to severe. The event covers southern Ohio, which includes {county} County.

NOAA's Ohio state climate summary says a prolonged heat wave affected the Ohio River Valley from July 17 to 24, 2011. It also says high temperatures combined with high humidity can create dangerous heat index values. The summary names extreme heat as a particular concern for the state's urban areas. {county} County is in the Southwest division of NOAA's Ohio climate divisions.

south_central.label: south central Ohio
climate: NOAA's Ohio state climate summary records that between March 1 and 3, 1997, 6 to 12 inches of rain fell in parts of southern Ohio. It also reports a significant increase in heavy rain events in Ohio, and it calls flood-producing rainstorms common in the warmer months. {county} County is in the South Central division of NOAA's Ohio climate divisions.

NWS Charleston's severe weather climatology covers part of southern Ohio and identifies April through July as the months when hail events cluster, with June the peak month. It reports that thunderstorm wind events are concentrated between April and August, and that hail events concentrate between 1 PM and 7 PM. Gallia, Jackson and Lawrence Counties are in its Ohio coverage and in the same division as {county} County.

The same NWS Charleston climatology says tornado events in its record cluster in the four months of April through July. It reports that tornadoes peak during the 5 to 6 PM hour and that the large majority of severe weather reports fall between 1 PM and 9 PM. These findings are for the Charleston forecast area, which includes Gallia, Jackson and Lawrence Counties of the South Central division that holds {county} County.

southeast.label: southeast Ohio
climate: NWS Charleston's severe weather climatology says the lack of rugged steep terrain plays a role in the density of tornadoes in southeast Ohio and along the Ohio River. Its coverage includes nine southeast Ohio counties, among them Athens, Meigs, Vinton, Perry, Gallia, Jackson and Lawrence. Its report covers hail, thunderstorm wind and tornado events. {county} County is in the Southeast division of NOAA's Ohio climate divisions.

The same climatology says the large majority of thunderstorm wind events in its record fall in the months from April to August. It also states that severe weather events concentrate between 1 PM and 9 PM, with hail peaking between 2 PM and 3 PM and tornadoes peaking in the 5 to 6 PM hour. Those findings describe the Charleston forecast area, which includes southeast Ohio counties near {county} County.

NWS Pittsburgh's severe weather climatology also covers Belmont, Guernsey and Monroe Counties, which are in the same Southeast division as {county} County. It uses tornado reports from 1950 to 2020 and severe wind and hail reports from 1955 to 2019. Its authors say a lot of cases go unrecorded, so report counts are a floor and not a full record.

Franklin.roofing:
Storm record for Franklin County

Count Franklin County's hail entries in NOAA's Storm Events Database and you get 92 reports on 32 separate days, the first from April 2016 and the last from June 2026. Fifty of the 92, on 21 of those days, give a stone diameter of 1.00 inch or larger. Dublin on September 1, 2019 and Westerville on July 24, 2023 share the top figure of 1.75 inches; the Dublin entry reads "Several reports of 1 to 1.75 inch diameter hail were received from the Dublin area." Four entries sit one step lower at 1.50 inches: Grove City on April 3, 2018, Minerva Park on July 24, 2023, Grove City again on February 28, 2024 ("Two separate reports of ping pong sized hail were received in the Grove City area") and Westerville on March 22, 2026.

The entries pile up on a few afternoons. April 17, 2024 carries 10 reports naming Dublin, Gahanna, Grandview Heights, Westerville and the Columbus airport that NOAA still labels Port Columbus, none larger than 1.00 inch. April 3, 2018 and July 15, 2024 carry 8 each. The 2018 date spreads across Canal Winchester, Grove City, Groveport and Pleasant Corners; the 2024 date runs from Pleasant Corners and Shadeville up to Marble Cliff, with four entries in Grandview Heights. Twenty-seven hail reports on 5 days make 2024 the heaviest year in the file. Sorted by month for April 2016 through June 2026, April leads with 33 reports on 6 days, July follows with 23 on 7 days and March has 15 on 6 days; the other five months with any hail share 21 reports. NOAA marks the 2026 entries as preliminary.

On the wind side, the file holds 169 thunderstorm wind reports on 78 days between March 2016 and June 2026. A measured gust accompanies 23 of them; the other 146 carry an estimated figure. June (50 reports on 18 days) and July (43 reports on 22 days) together hold 93 reports on 40 of the days. June 10, 2020 is the busiest single day with 13 reports; its Linworth entry says Linworth Road and OH-161 were closed because of trees down.

Winds that are not tied to a thunderstorm are filed separately. NOAA's file lists 15 High Wind and 5 Strong Wind reports for Franklin County from April 3, 2016 through March 15, 2026, and warns that such events are filed under forecast zones and may be missing. The March 13, 2026 High Wind entry reads "The Columbus ASOS measured a gust to 69 mph, and the AWOS station at Rickenbacker measured a gust to 63 mph."

NOAA's database holds 9 tornado reports on 5 days in the county between June 2016 and March 2025. The EF0 filed under Columbus on June 4, 2016 opens its narrative on Deserette Court. The EF1 of April 3, 2018 touched down just south of Orders Road in Grove City, crossed Hoover Road and I-71 and lifted short of Stringtown Road. An EF1 filed under Hanford on September 26, 2018 began in the Olde Towne neighborhood and ran on toward Bexley. Five reports share the early morning of February 28, 2024, all between 5:25 and 5:49 a.m. EST: an EF0 that crossed in from Madison County about 1.5 miles east southeast of West Jefferson; an EF1 that followed Roberts Road through Hilliard; an EF0 near Biggert Road and London Groveport Road; an EF0 that began in Walnut Woods Metro Park and left for Fairfield County across U.S. Route 33; and an EF2 filed under Blacklick, which began near Blacklick Elementary School in the Havens Corners area and moved through Havenswood toward McOwen Road. The ninth is an EF0 of March 30, 2025 that began south of I-270, west of Lockbourne Road.

Housing stock

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page estimates 616,365 housing units in Franklin County as of July 1, 2025 (Vintage 2025). The finer detail comes from table DP04 of the American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2020 to 2024, which counts 595,469 units, 553,099 of them occupied. Owners live in 292,123 of the occupied units (52.8 percent) and renters in 260,976 (47.2 percent).

By building type, that table lists 309,840 detached single-unit houses (52.0 percent of units), 58,811 attached single units (9.9 percent), 45,504 units in buildings of 3 or 4 units (7.6 percent) and 62,902 units in buildings of 20 or more (10.6 percent). By year built, it places 65,168 units (10.9 percent) in 1939 or earlier, 23,221 in the 1940s, 62,883 in the 1950s, 69,128 in the 1960s and 86,026 in the 1970s, the largest of the decade bands at 14.4 percent. Those five bands add up to 306,426 units built before 1980, or 51.5 percent. A roof on a 1960s house has had more years to reach replacement age than one on a 2010s house, so find out when yours was last redone.

Permits and local rules

Columbus Building and Zoning Services settles the question on its Frequently Asked Questions page: "The replacement of a roof, siding, windows or doors require a Roof, Siding, Windows, Doors permit." The same page says "This permit only comes with one inspection" and that inspections can be scheduled "through our Citizen Access Portal or automated phone system." The department's Typical Residential Projects sheet (revision BA 3/26) puts "Replace roof" under "Requires a permit, but not plan review." Neither page gives a layer limit or an ice barrier rule, so ask the department at 614-645-7433.

The Department of Commerce describes the Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board as licensing "electrical, HVAC, plumbing, hydronics and refrigeration commercial contractors." A roofer does not appear in that list, and inside Columbus the credential comes from the city, which calls it a license. Columbus defines a Home Improvement Contractor category for structural work on an existing one, two or three family dwelling, plus a Home Improvement - Limited Contractor category for work "limited to a specific scope (ex: roofing, decks, fencing, etc.)." Its application sheet asks a limited contractor for "a minimum of one (1) full year of 'hands-on' experience in that field." The Citizen Access Portal has a "Search for a Contractor" link under General Information.

Outside Columbus, the Franklin County Building Department says it is "responsible for issuing building permits for 1-, 2- and 3-family residential structures and associated development." For Brown, Clinton, Franklin, Hamilton, Madison, Mifflin, Norwich, Pleasant, Sharon and Truro townships, it says projects must apply for a Certificate of Zoning Compliance through the county's Economic Development and Planning Department. Re-roofing is not mentioned on that page, so put the roof question to the county department directly.

What to line up before you ask for bids

- A paper or PDF copy of any written estimate from your insurer.

- Which office issues roof permits at your address: Columbus Building and Zoning Services, the county department, or the building office of your own city or village.

- For a Columbus address, a look at the portal's "Search for a Contractor" list to see how each bidder appears there.

Cuyahoga.roofing:
Storm record for Cuyahoga County

The hail file for Cuyahoga County in NOAA's Storm Events Database starts on March 30, 2017 and runs to June 2026: 62 reports on 18 separate days, with none logged for 2016. April and May together hold 32 of the 62 reports on 8 days, and July adds 13 on 3 days. January 8, 2019 is the one winter date, with 6 reports from places such as Cuyahoga County Airport, where half dollar sized hail is noted, and Strongsville, where an NWS employee and a member of the public reported one inch hail.

The biggest stones are recent. On April 15, 2026, NOAA's database holds 12 hail reports filed under Bedford, Bedford Heights, Maple Heights, Middleburg Heights, Moreland Hills, Parma, Parma Heights, Solon and Walton Hills. Two of them, in Bedford and Solon, give 2.25 inches, the largest in the file; the Bedford entry mentions a picture of a hailstone 2.25 inches across, measured with a ruler. Earlier 2.00-inch reports are listed for Newburgh Heights on April 7, 2020 and Westlake on July 20, 2023. That July 2023 afternoon logs 10 reports in all, with 1.75 inches in Parma Heights and 1.50 inches in Parma, Brooklyn, Seven Hills and Valley View. The year 2025 brings 12 reports on 4 days, led by May 1 (Lyndhurst, Highland Heights, Solon and Mayfield among them). The 2026 file was compiled on September 18, 2026 and is preliminary, so 2026 counts may change.

Wind produces the longer list: 219 thunderstorm wind reports on 71 days between May 2016 and June 2026. June, July and August hold 133 of them on 42 days, and August alone has 72 on 13 days. August 6, 2024 stands out with 32 reports, including 75-knot estimated gusts listed for Cleveland and Parma Heights. The November 5, 2017 entry, filed under Strongsville Airport, describes a downburst with gusts of "at least 85 mph" whose path began at the county line west of Strongsville and ran east through North Royalton, Broadview Heights, Brecksville and Chagrin Falls. For August 11, 2021, an off-duty NWS meteorologist estimated a peak gust of 75 mph about two miles west-northwest of Bay Village. Gusts that are not tied to a thunderstorm are filed as High Wind or Strong Wind: 22 reports, among them a 67 mph gust at Cleveland Hopkins Airport on February 24, 2019.

Six tornado reports fall on 3 days between June 2019 and August 2024. The EF1 of June 16, 2019 touched down just east of the I-271 and I-480 junction near Oakwood and lifted near Glenwillow about two miles on. On August 24, 2023, an EF1 with estimated peak winds of 110 mph began near East 71st Street and Chester Avenue and ended near 89th Street and Euclid Avenue, while an EF2 at an estimated 120 mph, filed under Bedford Heights, began along Vera Street just east of Green Road, crossed the I-271 and I-480 interchange and emerged across Galaxy Parkway. On August 6, 2024, two EF1 tornadoes, each at an estimated 110 mph, crossed Bay Village, one entering from Lorain County just west of Wolf Road, and a third began near Sylvia Drive in Brook Park at an estimated 104 mph. These are reports of weather events and say nothing about any particular address.

Housing stock

The American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2020 to 2024 (Census Bureau table DP04) count 615,331 housing units in Cuyahoga County, 554,551 of them occupied. Owners live in 329,173 occupied units (59.4 percent) and renters in 225,378 (40.6 percent). Detached single-unit houses number 365,283, also 59.4 percent of all units; the same table lists 43,885 units in two-unit buildings (7.1 percent) and 92,249 units in buildings of 20 or more (15.0 percent).

The year-built rows lean old. Buildings from 1939 or earlier hold 171,286 units (27.8 percent), the 1940s hold 55,584 (9.0 percent), the 1950s hold 116,518 (18.9 percent), the 1960s hold 88,873 (14.4 percent) and the 1970s hold 62,613 (10.2 percent). Added together, that is 494,874 units, or 80.4 percent of the 2020 to 2024 total, built before 1980. Only 3,705 units (0.6 percent) date from 2020 or later. A house that old can have several generations of roof behind it, so the age of yours is worth pinning down first.

Permits and local rules

Cleveland's Department of Building and Housing says "a residential permit is required to reroof, apply siding, install gutters, doors, and windows." Its Division of Construction Permitting issues permits and registers contractors. The department's home-building page says "contractors must be bonded, insured and registered" to build or rehabilitate Cleveland homes, and gives 216.664.2884 for registration. It adds that "Owner-occupants of one- or two-family homes may perform alterations or build homes without being registered as contractors but are subject to the same regulations that apply to contractors for permits, plan examination, and inspection." Homeowners who have hired a contractor "should call 216.664.2910 to verify that their contractor is registered and should ask the contractor for copies of all permits before work begins." On inspections, "Contractors and do-it-yourselfers are responsible for scheduling inspections by calling the office number listed on the building permit," and work "should not be accepted prior to final inspection by a Building and Housing inspector." Layers and ice barrier are not addressed on those pages; ask the department.

Cleveland's rules stop at the city line. Parma Heights publishes its own roof permit application that offers tear-off and re-roof options, says "One re-roof allowed (2 layers)" and says "Ice guard required." It lists 440-884-9607 for the Parma Heights Building Department. Elsewhere in the county, the local building office is the one to ask.

The Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board's page names the trades it licenses: electrical, HVAC, plumbing, hydronics and refrigeration. Roofing is absent, and in Cleveland a roofer registers with the Division of Construction Permitting.

What to line up before you ask for bids

- A copy of your insurer's estimate, if one exists.

- The number of layers on your roof now and its age, since Parma Heights allows one re-roof and your own city may set a different limit.

- The name of your building department; in Cleveland, call 216.664.2910 to confirm a contractor's registration.

- From the contractor you hire, copies of all permits before work begins, as Cleveland's department advises.

Hamilton.roofing:
Storm record in Hamilton County

Hamilton County's hail tally in NOAA's Storm Events Database stands at 57 reports on 20 distinct days between April 2016 and March 2025, and NOAA's 2026 data is preliminary. March and April hold 34 of the 57 reports and 10 of the 20 days, 18 reports in March and 16 in April. Two dates tie for the busiest, at 8 reports each: March 1, 2017, with entries that include Harrison, Dent, New Baltimore, Mt. Healthy, the former Blue Ash airport site and Montgomery, and December 1, 2018, with entries that include Rendcomb Junction, Silverton, Deer Park, Montgomery, Sixteen Mile Stand and an east side Cincinnati point that NOAA labels Dayton. April 26, 2016 adds 5 more, from Delhi Hills, Forestville, Cherry Grove, Sweetwine and Elizabethtown.

The Harrison entry carries the largest size, 2.00 inches; NOAA's narrative reads "Hail of 1 to 2 inches in diameter was reported in the Harrison area." Next comes 1.50 inches at the former Blue Ash airport site on April 8, 2020. Seven reports list 1.25-inch hail: Forestville (April 26, 2016), Deer Park and Silverton (December 1, 2018), Woodlawn (April 8, 2020), Mt. Summit and Cherry Grove (May 23, 2020) and NOAA's "Dayton" point in east side Cincinnati (July 2, 2023). The year 2020 holds the largest yearly hail total, 13 reports on 4 days.

Thunderstorm wind outnumbers hail by a wide margin: 149 reports on 73 distinct days between March 2016 and June 2026, with May, June and July holding 96 of the reports and 51 of the days. April 8, 2020 is the heaviest wind date, with 15 reports, the same date as the Blue Ash airport hail. The highest estimated gust is 87 knots at Covedale on July 13, 2016, where NOAA's narrative places an area of straight-line winds stretching from eastern Westwood east into the Clifton area. Only 15 of the 149 reports carry a measured gust, 11 of them from Lunken Field; the highest measured gust is 66 knots at Lunken Field on August 4, 2018. On May 21, 2022, a boat video showed a gustnado, a brief whirl on a thunderstorm's outflow, moving north across the Ohio River and coming ashore in Sayler Park, with the entry naming Catalpa Road, Gracely Drive and Fernbank Avenue. Non-thunderstorm gusts are filed separately, 10 High Wind and 7 Strong Wind reports, including a 69 mph gust at Lunken Field on March 30, 2022.

Four tornado reports, all rated EF0, fall on three days between July 2016 and April 2020. The Covedale track of July 13, 2016 opens in NOAA's narrative at the intersection of Queen City Avenue and Westbrook Drive, then continues between Werk Road and Westbrook Drive toward Boudinot Avenue. The Mt. Washington track of March 1, 2017 began in a wooded ravine between 4 Mile Road and Phillips Road. On April 8, 2020, the Bevis tornado touched down in Colerain Township near Colerain Avenue and followed Compton Road into the center of Mt. Healthy, and the Silverton tornado began along Keller Road and dissipated along Park Road. These reports say nothing about any particular address and are not a forecast.

Housing stock

QuickFacts from the U.S. Census Bureau estimates 383,689 housing units in Hamilton County as of July 1, 2025. In the American Community Survey 5-year table DP04 for 2020 to 2024, the count is 381,356 units, with 354,739 occupied. Owners live in 210,407 of the occupied units (59.3 percent) and renters in 144,332 (40.7 percent). Detached single-unit houses number 222,028 (58.2 percent of units); the table also lists 28,818 units in buildings of 3 or 4 units (7.6 percent) and 38,995 in buildings of 20 or more (10.2 percent).

By year built, the 2020 to 2024 table puts 94,778 units (24.9 percent) in 1939 or earlier, 24,830 in the 1940s, 55,561 in the 1950s, 54,799 in the 1960s and 47,064 in the 1970s. Those five bands sum to 277,032 units, 72.6 percent of the total, built before 1980. Units from 2010 to 2019 number 16,951 (4.4 percent). The longer a house has stood, the more roof cycles it has been through, so check the age of yours before you plan.

Permits and local rules for a roof replacement

The City of Cincinnati's Department of Buildings and Inspections publishes a permit guide. Its "Do I Need A Permit?" step says "Generally, you don't need a permit for these projects at 1-, 2- and 3-family detached dwellings," and the list includes "Roof coverings (no more than two layers of roofing material)." For anything beyond two layers, or a different kind of building, call the department at (513) 352-3271. The guide states no ice barrier rule, and it adds an exception: for a locally designated historic property, a "Certificate of Appropriateness" must be obtained from the Urban Conservator (513-352-4848) before work, even if the work would otherwise be exempt.

The contractor registration page says the City "requires all contractors performing work in the City of Cincinnati limits, to maintain a current contractor registration, which must be renewed on an annual basis," and exempts the owner of a 1-, 2- or 3-family dwelling "as long as the homeowner personally performs the work upon the premises and will occupy the residence for at least one year after the work is complete." The guide links the City's Find a Registered Contractor lookup. Permit applications go through the City's Permit Center at 805 Central Ave., Suite 500, which lists hours of 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Outside Cincinnati the rules depend on the address. Hamilton County Buildings and Inspections, part of Planning and Development, describes itself as "responsible for issuing building permits in the unincorporated townships of Hamilton County and in six contract jurisdictions." Its page offers a Track Permit/Inspection lookup and lists 513-946-4550.

The Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board licenses "electrical, Heating Ventilating and Air Conditioning (HVAC), plumbing, hydronics and refrigeration contractors." Roofing is not named there, so a roofer's registration inside Cincinnati is the City's, as the registration page says.

What to line up before you ask for bids

- The age of your roof and its number of layers, since Cincinnati's exemption refers to two.

- Your address's jurisdiction: City of Cincinnati, another city or village, or Hamilton County Buildings and Inspections.

- Whether your home is a locally designated historic property, a question for the Urban Conservator before any bid is accepted.

- A written answer from each bidder on who pulls the permit, if one is needed, and the exact company name to check in the Find a Registered Contractor lookup.

- Any written document from your insurer about the roof, shared with each bidder.
